headline: High-risk workspace overlap and cascading action paths: both agents can write the same files, run shells, and use MCP, creating dangerous default conflict and trust chains.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: Both agents can read/write workspace files and use MCP, so one agent can place content the other may later parse as instructions. Cline’s shared_state_with_other_instances is via filesystem, and ECC’s shared_state warns about separate roots to avoid overwriting session files. This is a plausible default bridge, though not proven to be instruction-parsing by default.
conditions: IF both agents operate in the same workspace or shared root
IF either agent reads untrusted file content as instructions or tool directives
mitigations: Use separate workspace roots for each agent
Disable shared filesystem handoff between agents
Require manual review of any file one agent writes for the other
Restrict MCP servers to trusted, provenance-tagged sources
requires-engineering: add content provenance labels to inter-agent files

B_data_leakage.rationale: Cline touches source code and browser screenshots, while ECC touches session summaries, learned skills, hooks, and security findings. Both have filesystem access and broad/allowlisted network egress, so sensitive workspace data can flow into outputs or external APIs in default setups. The pair does not prove PHI, but the shared workspace plus networked tooling makes leakage plausible.
conditions: IF both agents are pointed at the same repository or home-directory workspace
IF either agent forwards file contents or session summaries to its backend or external APIs
mitigations: Separate sensitive and non-sensitive workspaces
Turn off network access for tasks that do not need it
Review which files each agent may read before execution
Redact secrets from shared session summaries
requires-engineering: enforce per-agent data-loss-prevention filters

C_capability_conflict.rationale: Both agents can execute shells, install packages, modify git state, read/write the filesystem, and use MCP. Cline explicitly shares state via filesystem, and ECC warns about separate roots to avoid overwriting session files. That overlapping write surface creates a default conflict path with possible git corruption or lost edits unless externally coordinated.
conditions: IF both agents are active in the same git checkout or shared filesystem root
IF either agent writes files or git state without an external lock
mitigations: Assign each agent a separate checkout or root directory
Serialize git writes with a manual lock file
Pause one agent before the other edits the same branch
Limit package installs to one designated agent
requires-engineering: add workspace-level locking and conflict detection

D_cascading_error.rationale: ECC’s workflow centers on skills and specialized subagents, while Cline is an autonomous coding agent with browser and shell tools. If Cline produces code or findings that ECC then treats as authoritative, errors can cascade into commits, hooks, or downstream actions. The pair’s default autonomy makes unverified handoff risky.
conditions: IF Cline output is fed into ECC skills or subagents without verification
IF ECC uses Cline-produced findings to modify files, hooks, or git history
mitigations: Require a human review step between agents
Force ECC to cite source files before acting on Cline output
Disable auto-commit or auto-apply steps
Use a checklist for any downstream action based on prior-agent output
requires-engineering: add structured validation of upstream outputs

E_compliance.rationale: ECC explicitly handles session summaries, hooks, security findings, and retention-related secrets, while Cline handles source code and browser screenshots. Both are docs-only and not tied to a specific residency regime, but the differing retention and data-handling surfaces create a compliance mismatch risk if the same regulated data class is routed through both.
conditions: IF regulated data is stored in the shared workspace or session summaries
IF retention or deletion requirements differ between the two agents' storage paths
mitigations: Keep regulated data out of shared agent workspaces
Set short retention for session summaries
Review which secrets each agent may persist
Document a single data owner for the pair
requires-engineering: map each data class to a residency and retention policy
